This survey introduces the Instructor-Student (I-S) architecture, a prominent framework for knowledge learning in deep neural networks (DNNs) designed to reduce computational complexity. Within this model, the network is divided into two parts: a lightweight "Instructor" used for training and a heavy "Student" used for inference. The process occurs in two phases: first, the Instructor is trained on the full dataset; second, the Student is trained on the Instructor's predictions alongside the original data. Unlike conventional methods that require co-training on massive datasets, the I-S architecture allows the Student to learn from both real labels and the Instructor's outputs, effectively treating the Instructor's predictions as a new dataset. This enables the Student to be trained on data points predicted by the Instructor, even when their true labels are unknown. We provide a comprehensive overview of the I-S architecture, categorizing relevant DNN knowledge learning methods by their knowledge source (classification, regression, or relation prediction) and presenting a detailed comparison of various I-S based models. Furthermore, we explore broader applications of this architecture beyond knowledge distillation, summarize existing evaluation metrics, and identify future research directions. To support these discussions, we propose a set of commonly used metrics for assessing DNN knowledge learning, hoping to establish standardized metrics for this specific architecture. Finally, we provide detailed descriptions of commonly used datasets and summarize existing surveys on knowledge distillation, offering guidance for future work in this architecture. The I-S architecture represents a versatile framework applicable across diverse domains, tasks, and architectures, serving as an effective solution for reducing a student's computational complexity without sacrificing accuracy. By allowing students to be trained on datasets predicted by instructors—even when ground truth labels are unavailable—this architecture offers significant advantages over traditional approaches. We hope this survey attracts researchers to investigate this architecture for various tasks, particularly in vision-language tasks and large language models. To facilitate this, we introduce an open-source repository at https://github.com/SHREYAS-1009/IS-Architecture containing commonly used datasets and methods for this architecture, aimed at standardizing research in this area. The repository includes datasets such as SNLI, multiNLI, SST-2, MRPC, MNLI, and others, alongside methods like MD, MI, and MD-MS. We anticipate that this architecture and the associated repository will be utilized for different tasks and datasets, potentially yielding significant results. A graph $G=(V,E)$ equipped with geodesic distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is considered truncated at level $k$ if $d(u,\alpha)$ is deemed a third level for all $u\in V$ and $\alpha\notin V$, where $d(u,\alpha)>k$. This perspective yields a metric space $(V,\rho_k)$ defined by $\rho_k(u,\alpha)=\min\{d(u,\alpha),k\}$, giving rise to the trimmed metric $\rho_k$. Consequently, standard metric concepts can be redefined under this trimmed metric; for instance, a set $S\subseteq V$ acts as a trimmed resolving set for $G$ if, for every pair of distinct vertices $u,\alpha$, there exists a vertex $s\in S$ such that $\rho_k(s,u)\neq\rho_k(s,\alpha)). The smallest cardinality of such a resolving set $(V,\rho_k)$ is termed the trimmed metric dimension of $G$, denoted by $\delta_{k}(G)$. This article examines several graph families to determine their trimmed metric dimension, establishes specific bounds, and explores the associated properties. The study highlights that the trimmed metric dimension is inherently linked to the graph's diameter, degree, and classic invariant dimensions. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of a trimmed metric basis and defines a corresponding hierarchy of trimmed metric bases.

Mathematical models of epidemic dynamics serve as a vital link between theoretical insights into disease transmission and the practical implementation of public health interventions. This article offers a comprehensive review of current models used during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, emphasizing the inherent difficulties in constructing a model suitable for the complex, real-time application of epidemic response measures. Ideally, a hierarchy of models ranging from simplified to complex structures should be employed in practice, allowing detailed, mechanistic models to inform strategies while simpler, agile models are utilized for actual real-time decision-making. Ultimately, regardless of the complexity involved in building and running these models, significant uncertainties remain concerning transmission mechanisms, initial conditions, and the specific goals of intervention measures during the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic and future epidemics. These uncertainties, coupled with the high stakes of epidemic response decisions, necessitate the careful consideration of multiple distinct models and the associated uncertainties regarding transmission mechanisms and intervention objectives to optimize public health outcomes. Furthermore, as societies relax restrictions during the current pandemic and as future epidemics occur, significant investments are required to optimize models, mechanisms, and response strategies for the greatest possible health benefits.

Software testing holds significant value within the verification community but remains underutilized in industrial settings due to the high cost of defects. From a theoretical standpoint, automated tools like static analyzers and model checkers represent the extreme of a geometric approach to verification, where feasible code executions are treated as a "shape" constrained by semantic rules, and correctness is ensured by proving this shape fits within a predefined correct shape. Experimental results from C# programs demonstrate that AutoTest produces more rigorous tests than traditional dynamic approaches. The findings further indicate that automatic unit testing can be deeply integrated into developer workflows, offering an affordable layer of assurance without replacing formal verification for certified software. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. To gather data, an array of loudspeakers placed inside the cavity excites the sound field, while an array of accelerometers on the exterior records the resulting velocity field. A specific inversion approach is employed to refine a Rayleigh-Plesset boundary condition model by optimizing a cost function derived from a deep neural network that maps the excited sound field to the boundary's normal velocity. Utilizing an L-shaped cavity, the experiment involves exciting the sound field with ten loudspeakers and detecting it with twenty-one accelerometers. The results show that the material loss factors of the three panels constituting the cavity can be accurately identified (within two percent), and the spatial mode of the sound field before and after inversion is correctly reconstructed. Furthermore, the material loss factors of the panels are linearly correlated with the first modal acoustic loss factor of the cavity, which is correctly recovered after inversion. Finally, the material loss factors can also be correctly identified in the dark using only a single loudspeaker and a single accelerometer. (Author's abstract)

We introduce the simplest variant of scoto-seesaw Model B, which features a single additional see-saw scale and the minimal super-scenario for stabilizing the Higgs vacuum. We explicitly detail the model's particle content and interaction Lagrangians, demonstrating that one see-saw scale and two right-handed neutrons are required to generate two distinct mixing angles via the seesaw mechanism necessary for triangular closure. Leveraging open-source software, we first map out the valid parameter space, including a detailed analysis of the mass eigenvalues. Subsequently, we conduct comprehensive phenomenological studies, specifically examining vacuum stability and collider constraints. With straightforward extensions, we perform a thorough analysis of dark matter phenomenology, for which we have developed a specialized module within MicrOMEGAs. Ultimately, we establish the intricate interplay between dark matter stability, co-annihilation regions, and collider limits. Our findings indicate that within the minimal framework, dark matter must reside in the focus-point region, where the lightest neutralino has predominantly neutral-longitudent neutrino (LNV) character. Finally, we report that the first direct detection experiment, XENONnT, has eliminated all feasible parameter points for this model. While extended models with multiple see-saw scales and two layers of R-seesaw can easily satisfy all constraints, such configurations represent significant theoretical and phenomenological departures from the principles of micro-megascale simplicity that motivate these models. As a direct consequence of our analysis, the simplest B-type scoto-seesaw model, along with the simplest A-type variant, cannot be tested at LHC Run 3 or future 100 TeV colliders, as their lowest constraints exceed the capabilities even of hypothetical 1 PeV colliders. Given that such models offer no unique benefits over other alternatives, we conclude that the simplest B-type scoto-seesaw model should be considered replaced by other theoretical frameworks. To facilitate future investigations into stabilizing neutrino masses and mixing angles beyond the minimal scoto-seesaw approaches, we have made all our models, their constraints, and correlations a public tool known as the Neutrino Mass and Mixing Mosaic (N4MMM), available at https://github.com/BNagy1/N4MMM. This mosaic tool will enable future research to explore the feasible parameter spaces of various models to address the mass and mixing angle puzzles, whether through further theoretical work or at future theoretical meetings.
